title: AI Helps Harvard Mathematician Disprove 87-Year-Old Jacobian Conjecture in a Single Tweet
excerpt: Levent Alpöge used Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 to crack one of mathematics' most stubborn unsolved problems — and announced it casually on X during the World Cup final.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Levent Alpöge disproved the Jacobian conjecture, unresolved since 1939, using AI in a tweet.
  • The counterexample is 216 characters long and verified by multiple mathematicians.
  • This achievement is considered the most significant AI contribution to mathematics so far.
  • The conjecture is false for three or more dimensions, but remains unsolved in two dimensions.
AI Breakthrough in Mathematics
›Jacobian conjecture proposed in 1939.
›Counterexample produced in less than a day.
›Counterexample verified by multiple mathematicians.
›AI models now act as research collaborators.

A Harvard mathematician has disproved one of the most stubborn unsolved problems in algebra — with help from an AI model and a casually worded post on X that arrived while the rest of the world was watching the World Cup final.

Levent Alpöge, a 33-year-old junior fellow at Harvard University, announced on July 20 that the Jacobian conjecture — a famous proposition in algebraic geometry that has defied resolution since 1939 — is false. His proof: a single counterexample, just 216 characters long, produced in collaboration with Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.

"Hello there the Jacobian conjecture is false thanks to my close friend akhil for asking about it and my other close friend fable for working during the world cup final."

— Levent Alpöge, on X

What the Jacobian Conjecture Actually Says

The Jacobian conjecture, first proposed by German mathematician Ott-Heinrich Keller in 1939, deals with polynomial mappings — mathematical functions built from basic operations like addition, subtraction, and multiplication (but not division). The conjecture proposes that if such a mapping passes a specific reversibility test (having a nonzero constant Jacobian determinant), then the mapping itself should be fully reversible using polynomials.

> **"According to Fast Company, others used OpenAI's GPT models for additional cross-checks, sometimes producing "unintentionally hilarious results" in the process.

![World Cup."** https://x.com/VaibhavSisinty/status/2079208461141966859

In simpler terms: imagine using a formula to rearrange all the points on a map. The conjecture says that if the formula does not crush or flatten anything, you should always be able to undo it with another formula of the same kind. Alpöge showed this is not always true, at least in three or more dimensions.

The problem appeared on Stephen Smale's influential 1998 list of "Mathematical Problems for the Next Century," and mathematician T.T. Moh predicted in 2008 that a solution could take humans "another 100 years." It took an AI-assisted effort less than a day.

A Counterexample That Fits in a Tweet

Alpöge's counterexample is a polynomial mapping from three-dimensional complex space to itself. The formula, which maps three variables through a set of polynomial equations, has a constant Jacobian determinant of -2 — meaning it passes the conjecture's reversibility test — yet it sends three distinct input points to the same output, proving it cannot be reversed. The entire expression fits comfortably in a single social media post.

Several mathematicians have already independently verified the result using SymPy, a Python library for symbolic mathematics, and Lean, a formal proof assistant. According to Fast Company, others used OpenAI's GPT models for additional cross-checks, sometimes producing "unintentionally hilarious results" in the process.

Verified by Multiple Mathematicians

Abhishek Saha, a mathematician at Queen Mary University of London, told New Scientist that this is "probably the biggest conjecture that AI has played a significant role in proving or disproving so far in mathematics."

The result follows a string of AI-driven mathematical achievements in 2026. In May, an unreleased OpenAI model helped settle an 80-year-old geometry problem posed by Paul Erdős. Earlier, Anthropic's Claude assisted physicists in proving a 10-year-old conjecture about jamming in disordered materials.

AI models are increasingly functioning as genuine research collaborators rather than mere calculators. Researchers now use them to suggest proof strategies, fill logical gaps, check arguments for errors, and translate proofs into computer-verifiable languages. The speed at which counterexamples and proofs can be generated is compressing decades of mathematical exploration into weeks.

What Remains Unsolved

Alpöge's result disproves the Jacobian conjecture for three or more dimensions, but the two-dimensional case — the original and most studied formulation — remains open. The counterexample does not extend downward, meaning mathematicians still do not know whether every polynomial mapping in two variables with a constant nonzero Jacobian determinant is invertible.

The work has not yet undergone formal peer review, though the brevity of the counterexample makes verification straightforward. As Saha noted, the result is "simple to verify and many mathematicians have already done so."

For the broader scientific community, the implications extend well beyond algebra. If frontier AI models can dismantle problems that have resisted the world's best mathematicians for nearly a century, the pace of discovery in physics, cryptography, and engineering could accelerate dramatically in the years ahead.
